t.6.36.1: Then the forest-dwellers, scanning both the sky and the earth, saw the two brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa covered all over with arrows.
t.6.36.3: Nīla, Dvivida and Mainda, and Suṣeṇa, Sumukha and Aṅgada, together with Hanumān, swiftly began to grieve for the two Rāghavas.
t.6.36.2: When the rākṣasa, his deed accomplished, had withdrawn, like the rain-god falling still after pouring down his rain, Vibhīṣaṇa, together with Sugrīva, then came to that place.
t.6.36.4: Motionless, breathing faintly, drenched in streams of blood, covered with a mesh of arrows and rigid, the two lay upon their beds of arrows.
t.6.36.5: Breathing heavily like two serpents, motionless and with their strength grown feeble, their limbs smeared with streaming blood, the two lay like a pair of golden banners.
t.6.36.6: Those two heroes lay upon the bed of heroes, scarcely able to move, surrounded by those troop-leaders whose eyes were troubled with tears.
t.6.36.7: Seeing the two Rāghavas fallen, covered over by a net of arrows, all the vānaras together with Vibhīṣaṇa became distressed.
t.6.36.8: Though the monkeys scanned the sky and all the directions, they could not see Rāvaṇi in the battle, for he was concealed by his magic power.
t.6.36.9: But Vibhīṣaṇa, looking about by means of magic itself, then saw his brother's son standing there, concealed by magic.
t.6.36.10: By virtue of a boon, Vibhīṣaṇa saw that hero of incomparable deeds, unrivalled in battle, even though he had become invisible.
t.6.36.11: But Indrajit, beholding his own deed and those two lying there, spoke, supremely delighted, gladdening all the Nairṛtas.
t.6.36.12: The two mighty brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, the slayers of Dūṣaṇa and of Khara, have been struck down by my arrows.
t.6.36.13: These two cannot be released from this bondage of arrows, not even by all the gods and asuras coming together along with the hosts of seers.
t.6.36.14: On whose account the three-watched night passes for my father, who, brooding and stricken with grief, does not touch his bed with his limbs.
t.6.36.16: All the valorous efforts of Rāma, of Lakṣmaṇa, and of all the forest-dwellers will prove fruitless, like clouds in autumn.
t.6.36.15: He on whose account this whole of Laṅkā is agitated like a river in the rainy season, that very calamity, the destroyer of the roots of all, has been slain by me.
t.6.36.17: Having spoken thus to all those rākṣasas standing at his sides, Rāvaṇi then struck all those troop-leaders as well.
t.6.36.18: Having tormented those monkeys with floods of arrows and having terrified them, the mighty-armed one laughed aloud and spoke these words.
t.6.36.19: Behold, O Rākṣasas, these two brothers together, bound by me at the head of the army with a terrible binding of arrows!
t.6.36.20: Thus addressed, all those rākṣasas, fighters by deceit, were filled with the greatest astonishment, gratified by that deed.
t.6.36.21: And all of them, like rain-clouds, roared great roars; knowing that Rāma was slain, they honored Rāvaṇi.
t.6.36.22: Then, seeing both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa lying motionless and breathless on the ground, he concluded, "They are slain."
t.6.36.23: Then Indrajit, victor in battle, filled with joy, entered the city of Laṅkā, gladdening all the Nairṛtas.
t.6.36.24: Seeing the bodies of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa covered with arrows, all their limbs both major and minor, fear entered Sugrīva.
t.6.36.25: Vibhīṣaṇa spoke to him, the lord of the monkeys, who was terrified and dejected, his face wet with tears and his eyes troubled by grief.
t.6.36.26: Enough of fear, O Sugrīva; let this flood of tears be checked. Battles are of this sort, and victory is never certain.
t.6.36.27: O hero, if any good fortune still remains for us, these two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, will shake off their swoon.
t.6.36.28: Steady yourself, O monkey, and steady me too, who am without a protector. For those devoted to truth and dharma there is no fear caused by death.
t.6.36.29: Having spoken thus, Vibhīṣaṇa then wiped the fair eyes of Sugrīva with a hand moistened with water.
t.6.36.30: Having wiped the face of that wise king of the monkeys, he spoke these calm words, suited to the moment.
t.6.36.31: O lord of the monkey kings, this is no time to give way to despondency. At this untimely hour, even excessive affection leads to death.
t.6.36.32: Therefore, casting aside this despondency, which ruins every undertaking, let the welfare of the armies led by Rāma be considered.
t.6.36.33: Or else, let Rāma be guarded for as long as his loss of consciousness lasts; once the two Kākutsthas have regained consciousness, they will dispel our fear.
t.6.36.35: Therefore compose yourself, and reassure your own forces as well, while I once more set all the troops back in their proper positions.
t.6.36.34: This is nothing at all to Rāma, nor is Rāma about to die, for the splendour that is hard to find among those whose life has ended will not abandon him.
t.6.36.36: For these monkeys, O bull among monkeys, their eyes wide open and seized with alarm out of terror, are whispering to one another from ear to ear.
t.6.36.38: Having comforted Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, then reassured once more that army of vānaras which had fled in panic.
t.6.36.37: But seeing me rushing forward to hearten the army, let the monkeys cast off their fear like a garland that has already been worn.
t.6.36.39: But Indrajit, the great master of illusion, surrounded by all his forces, entered the city of Laṅkā and went to his father.
t.6.36.40: There, saluting the seated Rāvaṇa with joined palms, he told his father the welcome news that Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa had been slain.
t.6.36.41: Then, hearing that his two foes had been struck down, Rāvaṇa sprang up in delight amid the rākṣasas and embraced his son.
t.6.36.42: Smelling him on the head, he, with a delighted heart, questioned him; and to his father, who was asking, he related everything just as it had happened.
t.6.36.43: His inner self swept by a surge of joy on hearing the words of that great chariot-warrior, he cast off the fever that had arisen on account of Dāśarathi, and, delighted, he praised his son with words.
